summary: An applicability statement for Classless Inter-Domain Routing, a way to slow the growth of routing tables and the use of new IP network numbers. It says what is needed to implement CIDR in the Internet. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1517 explains where Classless Inter-Domain Routing applies and which Internet domains are expected to support it. CIDR aims to slow the growth of routing tables by allowing routes to be expressed as address prefixes.

questions: which networks had to implement cidr
does cidr require one routing protocol
subtitle: Where the CIDR architecture applies and what routing domains are expected to support.

tldr.problem: The Internet faced rapid growth in routing tables and inefficient use of Class B network numbers, along with longer-term exhaustion of network numbers.
tldr.mechanism: CIDR uses address prefixes and aggregation to slow routing-table growth and reduce the need to allocate new network numbers.
tldr.outcome: The RFC requires backbone and transit domains to implement CIDR and recommends implementation by other domains; the unit metadata marks it Historic.

today: The unit metadata marks RFC 1517 as Historic. The document is an applicability statement for implementing CIDR in connected IP version 4 routing domains.

sections.title: Why CIDR Was Chosen
sections.content:
The RFC identifies three scaling concerns: inefficient use and possible exhaustion of Class B addresses, growth of routing information beyond what current router software and people could manage, and eventual exhaustion of IP network numbers.

CIDR is presented as a short- to mid-term response to the first two concerns. It aims to slow routing-table growth and reduce the need to allocate network numbers, but does not attempt to solve the longer-term exhaustion problem.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet was adding routes quickly and using some network numbers inefficiently. CIDR was selected to slow those problems while longer-term work continued.

sections.title: The CIDR Architecture
sections.content:
The RFC points to separate documents for the overall CIDR architecture and the address allocation and aggregation strategy. It also notes that inter-domain routing protocols need to handle reachability information expressed as IP address prefixes.

The applicability statement does not require one specific routing protocol. Domains that cannot propagate CIDR routes may need to send traffic for aggregated routes toward CIDR-capable parts of the Internet, which can limit the topology they support.
sections.plainLanguage: CIDR depends on routing systems being able to share address prefixes. This RFC does not require a particular routing protocol for doing so.

sections.title: Which Domains Must Implement CIDR
sections.content:
The CIDR architecture applies to connected domains that support IP version 4. It does not require every Internet domain to convert, and it assumes some domains will never do so, though routes to those places may be less optimal.

Domains providing backbone or transit service are required by this statement to implement CIDR fully. Other domains are strongly encouraged to do so, while remaining free to choose their internal and inter-domain routing designs.
sections.plainLanguage: Backbone and transit networks must implement CIDR under this statement. Other networks are strongly encouraged, but the RFC allows some domains to remain non-CIDR.
